pedagogy.summary: By Y5 children already know angle is an amount of turn measured in degrees (1/360 of a full turn). The protractor turns that idea into a tool skill: superimpose a fixed 'fan' of 180 one-degree angles onto the angle so its vertex sits at the centre and one ray runs along the zero line, then read where the second ray crosses the scale. The single hardest part is not the reading but the SET-UP (vertex on centre-cross, baseline on a ray) and CHOOSING WHICH of the two scales to read. Teach estimation-first: decide acute or obtuse before touching the protractor, so the read is checked against sense rather than trusted blindly. The Progressions recommend meeting a full-circle (360°) protractor before the standard two-scale semicircular one, so the connection to 'fraction of a turn' stays visible.
bestPractices: Estimate first: have the child say 'acute / right / obtuse' (and roughly how many degrees) BEFORE measuring, then use that to decide which scale to read — a 47° angle read as 133° is caught immediately because 133° is obviously not acute.
Teach placement as a two-part check every time: vertex exactly on the centre cross, AND one ray exactly along the 0-line; only then read the OTHER ray.
Rotate the angle into non-standard orientations from the start (ray pointing up, down, diagonal) so the child does not learn 'protractor only works when a ray is horizontal'.
When rays are drawn too short to reach the scale, extend the ray with a ruler first — reinforce that an angle's size does not depend on ray length.
Introduce a full-circle 360° protractor before the two-scale semicircle so degrees stay tied to fraction-of-a-turn; use a two-scale semicircular protractor once scale-choice is secure.
For drawing (e.g. 135°): mark the vertex and baseline, count up the correct scale to the target, mark a dot, then join — draw then check by re-measuring.
keyRepresentations: Protractor as a fixed fan of 180 one-degree unit angles laid over the angle (links directly to 'n one-degree angles = n degrees')
Full-circle 360° protractor (fraction-of-a-turn made visible) before the standard two-scale semicircular protractor
Benchmark angles (30°, 45°, 60°, 90°, 120°, 180°) used as an estimation check on the read
The acute-vs-obtuse decision as the rule for choosing the inner vs outer scale
commonMisconceptions: Reads the wrong scale — lands on the mirror value (e.g. 133° instead of 47°) because the child reads whichever number the ray crosses without checking acute/obtuse.
Believes the protractor only works when a ray is horizontal ('standard position') and cannot measure a rotated angle.
Measures the length of the rays or the gap between their ends rather than the rotation between them (arm-length carryover).
Does not extend rays that fall short of the scale arc, then reads a smaller/ambiguous value or gives up.

learn.summary: Teach protractor use as a placement-and-read procedure for measuring and drawing angles in whole-number degrees (Y5, ages 9–10). Learners already know an angle is an amount of turn measured in degrees (a full turn = 360°, so n one-degree turns = n degrees). The hard parts are the SET-UP (vertex exactly on the centre cross, one ray exactly along the 0-line) and CHOOSING which of the two scales to read. Lead with estimation: decide acute/right/obtuse (and roughly how many degrees) before measuring, then use that judgement to pick the scale and sanity-check the read. Meeting a full-circle 360° protractor before the standard two-scale semicircular one keeps the fraction-of-a-turn meaning visible. Target errors: reading the mirror value (133° for 47°), believing the tool only works when a ray is horizontal, judging size by ray length, and not extending short rays.

activities.title: Estimate-first measuring across orientations
feedback: If a reported number contradicts the angle's obvious type (an acute angle called 133°, or an obtuse one called 60°), pause: re-commit to acute/obtuse, compare against the 90° benchmark, then re-read the matching scale.

If the child turns the page or lines the baseline along the paper edge instead of along a ray, show the same angle rotated several ways and confirm it reads the same measure every time — placement follows the ray, not the page edge.

If readings are consistently a few degrees out in the same direction, check both parts of the placement: the baseline may be slightly rotated off the ray (a common cause of a steady offset), or the vertex may have slipped off the centre cross. Redo the two-part placement check.
On the short-ray angle, if the child reads a small/ambiguous value or says it is 'smaller because the lines are shorter', extend the rays with a ruler and re-measure to show the value is unchanged.
activities.rationale: Grade-level standards require measuring angles in whole-number degrees with a protractor and relating degrees to a fraction of a 360° circle. Documented difficulties — reading the wrong scale, failing on non-standard positions, and not extending rays — are directly rehearsed here, and estimate-first gives an independent check on the read.
sourceClaims: Grade 4 standard: measure angles in whole-number degrees using a protractor and sketch angles of specified measure (4.MD.6); the size of an angle is measured with reference to a circle, with the whole circle 360°, and an angle that turns through n one-degree angles has measure n degrees (4.MD.5).

Documented protractor difficulties: students read the wrong scale, struggle to measure angles that are not in standard position, and must learn that rays can be extended without changing the angle; a full-circle protractor is recommended before the two-scale semicircular one to keep the fraction-of-a-turn meaning visible.
Children commonly judge angle size by the length of the arms/rays rather than the amount of opening (turn), a persistent measurement misconception.
learnerActions: Before touching the protractor, say aloud whether each angle is acute, right, or obtuse, and give a rough degree estimate against benchmarks (30°, 45°, 60°, 90°, 120°, 180°).
Place the protractor so the vertex sits exactly on the centre cross AND one ray lies exactly along the 0-line — check both before reading anything.

Read the OTHER ray on the scale that starts at 0 on the ray you lined up, and check that the number matches your acute/obtuse estimate, then state the measure (e.g. report a rotated angle as 47°, not its mirror value 133°).
Repeat with angles drawn in non-standard orientations: a ray pointing up, down, and diagonally — do not rotate the paper to force a ray horizontal.
When rays are drawn too short to reach the scale arc, extend a ray with a ruler first, then measure; confirm the measure is the same before and after extending.
activities.intendedInsight: The measure is the amount of opening between the rays, read once the tool is correctly placed; it does not depend on ray length or on any ray being horizontal. The correct scale is the one that starts at 0 on the aligned ray; the acute/obtuse estimate (checked against the 90° benchmark) is a quick check that the right scale was read. For angles very close to 90° both scales read about the same, so careful placement decides the read.

activities.title: Full-circle before two-scale semicircle
feedback: If the child cannot say why one scale is chosen over the other, return to the full-circle tool and re-anchor the reading to the fraction of the turn.
If scale choice is still guessed, have them mark the 90° line first and decide acute/obtuse relative to it before reading.
activities.rationale: The progressions recommend meeting a full-circle protractor before the two-scale semicircular one so the fraction-of-a-turn meaning stays visible and scale choice becomes principled rather than memorised.
sourceClaims: Documented protractor difficulties: students read the wrong scale, struggle to measure angles that are not in standard position, and must learn that rays can be extended without changing the angle; a full-circle protractor is recommended before the two-scale semicircular one to keep the fraction-of-a-turn meaning visible.

Grade 4 standard: measure angles in whole-number degrees using a protractor and sketch angles of specified measure (4.MD.6); the size of an angle is measured with reference to a circle, with the whole circle 360°, and an angle that turns through n one-degree angles has measure n degrees (4.MD.5).
learnerActions: Measure several angles first on a full-circle (360°) protractor, reading the degrees as a fraction of a whole turn.
Then switch to the standard two-scale semicircular protractor and, for each angle, state whether you will read the inner or outer scale and why, before reading it.
Verbalise the link: '90° is a quarter turn; this angle is a bit less than a quarter so it is under 90°.'
activities.intendedInsight: Degrees are a fraction of a whole turn; the two scales on a semicircular protractor run in opposite directions, and the acute/obtuse judgement (checked against the 90° benchmark) is the main guide to which one applies — except for angles close to 90°, where both scales read near 90° and careful placement, not the acute/obtuse call, settles the read.

activities.title: Draw then check
feedback: If the drawn angle re-measures as 45° instead of 135°, the wrong scale was counted (45° and 135° are mirror values, 45+135=180) — re-identify acute/obtuse for the target and choose the scale deliberately.
If the vertex or baseline was not locked before marking, the dot will be placed off the true scale; redo the two-part placement check first.
activities.rationale: The standard requires sketching angles of specified measure, not only reading them; drawing then re-measuring closes the loop and reuses the same scale-choice and placement checks.
sourceClaims: Grade 4 standard: measure angles in whole-number degrees using a protractor and sketch angles of specified measure (4.MD.6); the size of an angle is measured with reference to a circle, with the whole circle 360°, and an angle that turns through n one-degree angles has measure n degrees (4.MD.5).
learnerActions: To draw a 135° angle: mark the vertex, draw a baseline, place the protractor (vertex on centre, baseline on 0-line).
Count UP the correct scale to 135°, mark a dot, and join the dot to the vertex.
Re-measure the angle you drew and confirm it reads about 135° (within ±2°); redraw if it is off.
Try drawing in a non-horizontal orientation too, so drawing is not tied to a baseline along the bottom of the page.
activities.intendedInsight: Drawing an angle is the inverse of measuring one: the same placement and scale-choice skills apply, and re-measuring your own drawing is a built-in check.

activities.title: Reasoning probes and reflex-angle stretch
feedback: If the child says 'that's the number the line hit' when asked why a scale was chosen, reteach estimate-first scale selection against the 90° benchmark.
If they treat the longer-armed angle as bigger, extend both pairs of rays to equal length and re-measure to show the measures are unchanged.

For 210°, acknowledge the semicircular scale physically stops at 180° so no single direct reading is possible; guide them to measure the smaller non-reflex angle of 150° and subtract from a full turn (360−150=210), or to use a full-circle 360° protractor.
activities.rationale: These prompts separate a real procedure from a brittle 'ray-along-the-bottom' ritual by surfacing the standard-position, ray-length, and wrong-scale misconceptions, and extend reasoning toward reflex angles beyond the semicircular scale.
sourceClaims: Children commonly judge angle size by the length of the arms/rays rather than the amount of opening (turn), a persistent measurement misconception.

Documented protractor difficulties: students read the wrong scale, struggle to measure angles that are not in standard position, and must learn that rays can be extended without changing the angle; a full-circle protractor is recommended before the two-scale semicircular one to keep the fraction-of-a-turn meaning visible.
learnerActions: Compare a rotated angle and a horizontal one and answer 'Which is bigger? How could you be sure without being told?' — justify by measuring, not by orientation.
Answer: 'If these two lines were made twice as long but opened the same, what would the protractor say?' and explain why the measure is unchanged.
Explain why you read one scale and not the other for a given angle.
Attempt to start drawing a 210° angle and explain what happens when the semicircular scale only runs to 180° (reasoning about reflex angles).
activities.intendedInsight: A secure measurer justifies readings by the amount of opening and by acute/obtuse scale choice, recognises ray length is irrelevant, and notices the semicircular scale's 180° limit when facing a reflex angle.

constraints: Learners must perform the placement themselves (physical protractor and paper, or a draggable/rotatable on-screen tool): reading a value off a pre-placed protractor, choosing inner-vs-outer scale, or identifying a measure in multiple-choice form practises sub-skills but does not assess the placement performance that is the core objective.
A static labelled diagram can name the parts of a protractor but cannot let the child place it, choose a scale, or recompute a reading; use it only as a reference, not as the main practice.
Include non-standard orientations from the start; do not let rotating the paper become a crutch that masks whether the child can align the baseline to any ray.
Include at least one short-ray angle so extending rays (and the ray-length-is-irrelevant idea) is explicitly rehearsed.

Interactive examples (snap/glow feedback when vertex-on-centre and baseline-on-ray are both met, a scale that lights based on the acute/obtuse choice, a draw-mode that re-measures the drawn angle) make the mechanism concrete but are optional implementations, not required.
Accuracy expectation is reading/drawing to within about ±2°.

The semicircular scale only runs to 180°; reflex angles (e.g. 210°) cannot be read directly from it and need separate reasoning (measure the 150° non-reflex angle and subtract from 360°, or use a full-circle protractor).
reviewNotes: This is an agent semantic rewrite of saved teaching research without fresh source verification; sources were NOT re-fetched. The activities are research-informed proposals, not validated interventions.

The legacy row asserted that only a 2D interactive tool teaches this skill and that a static image, a 3D environment, or a dialogue add nothing. These are catalog-preference claims, not established pedagogical laws, and have been softened: a physical protractor on paper is a fully valid medium, a static diagram can serve as a reference scaffold, and spoken reasoning can support (though not replace) hands-on placement practice.
The claim that measuring a planar angle in 3D 'adds no conceptual gain' is a design preference, not a verified finding; retained only as a scoped note that the task is inherently 2D.

The acute/obtuse-chooses-the-scale rule is faithful to the original keyRepresentations but is a heuristic; it is least reliable for angles close to 90°, where both scales read near 90° and placement accuracy, not the acute/obtuse call, settles the read. This caveat is now stated consistently in both the measuring and full-circle activities.

Arithmetic/logic self-audit: the 47°/133° and 45°/135° mirror pairs each sum to 180° (consistent with the two opposite-running scales), 360−150=210 for the reflex stretch, and the benchmark angles are internally consistent; no numeric errors found to correct.

probeDeeper: Point to the rotated angle and the horizontal one and ask: 'Which is bigger? How could you be sure without me telling you?' — listen for measuring rather than judging by orientation.
'You read 47°. If I made these two lines twice as long but kept them opened the same, what would the protractor say now?' (counterexample: ray length is irrelevant.)
'Why did you read this scale and not the other one?' — a secure child cites acute/obtuse; a brittle one says 'that's the number the line hit'.
'Show me how you'd start drawing a 210° angle' — surfaces whether they see the semicircular scale only goes to 180° and reason about reflex angles.
assess.correctAnswer: For each angle: vertex placed on the centre-cross, one ray on the 0-line, reads the scale that matches whether the angle is acute or obtuse (e.g. reports the rotated angle correctly rather than its mirror value), extends the short rays before reading, and reads to within ±2°. For the drawing: marks the vertex and baseline, counts up the correct scale, and draws an angle that re-measures to about 135°.

errorPatterns.pattern: Reads the wrong scale — reports the mirror value ('it's 133' for a clearly acute 47° angle) because they read whichever number the ray crosses without checking acute/obtuse.
errorPatterns.nextMove: Reinstate estimate-first: before every read, commit to acute or obtuse, then use that to pick the scale; check the read against a 90° benchmark. Reteach the degree-size sense if the acute/obtuse judgement itself is shaky.
errorPatterns.revealedBy: The reported number contradicts the angle's obvious type (calls an acute angle 133°, or an obtuse one 60°); often reads the inner scale for one angle and outer for the next with no rule.

errorPatterns.pattern: Can only measure when a ray is horizontal — rotates the paper or gives up on the angle drawn in non-standard orientation, believing the protractor 'only works' along the bottom.
errorPatterns.nextMove: Practise placing the baseline on a ray regardless of orientation; show the same angle rotated several times reads the same measure. Do NOT let the child rotate the paper as a crutch.
errorPatterns.revealedBy: Succeeds on the horizontal angle but turns the page, or places the baseline along the page edge instead of along a ray, for the rotated one.

errorPatterns.pattern: Measures ray length or the gap between the ray ends rather than the rotation — thrown by the short-ray angle, reads where the drawn ray stops or reports the longer-armed angle as bigger.
errorPatterns.nextMove: Extend the rays with a ruler and re-measure to show the value is unchanged; reconnect to angle as amount of turn, independent of ray length.
errorPatterns.revealedBy: On the short-rays angle they read a small/ambiguous value, or comment that it is 'smaller' because the lines are shorter, instead of extending the rays to the scale.

errorPatterns.pattern: Vertex off the centre-cross — lines the tool up on the 0-line but leaves the vertex short of or past the centre, so every reading is skewed.
errorPatterns.nextMove: Scaffold the two-part placement check (vertex-on-cross THEN ray-on-zero) as a habit; no reteaching of concept needed — the idea is held, the hand slips.
errorPatterns.revealedBy: Placement looks roughly right but readings are consistently a few degrees out in the same direction; the vertex visibly does not sit on the centre point.

responseLevels.gap: Cannot reliably place the protractor: vertex and baseline are not both aligned, readings are essentially random or copied from wherever a line crosses, and the drawn angle bears no relation to 135°.
responseLevels.full: Places vertex-on-centre and baseline-on-ray in any orientation, chooses the correct scale by first judging acute/obtuse, extends short rays, reads within ±2°, and draws a 135° angle that re-measures correctly — the procedure is robust across the varied set, not tied to a standard position.
responseLevels.partial: Measures correctly when a ray is already horizontal and reads a single scale, but is derailed by at least one of: a rotated angle (rotates the paper or misaligns), short rays (reads without extending), or scale choice (gives the mirror value). Can state the steps but cannot transfer them to the varied cases.

assess.diagnosticPrompt: Put three angles in front of the child, each drawn in a DIFFERENT orientation (one with a horizontal ray, one rotated so no ray is horizontal, one with rays drawn too short to reach the protractor's scale). Hand them a protractor and say: 'Measure each of these. Tell me the degrees.' Then give a blank and say: 'Now draw me an angle of exactly 135°.' Watch how they place the tool and choose the scale — do not explain the procedure.
assess.whatMakesItDiscriminate: The three deliberately-varied orientations separate a child who has a real procedure from one who has memorised a single 'ray-along-the-bottom' ritual: the rotated angle exposes the standard-position misconception, the short-rays angle exposes arm-length/ray-extension, and the acute-vs-obtuse spread exposes wrong-scale reading. A child measuring correctly for the right reasons handles all three; a child with a brittle routine succeeds only on the horizontal one.
